issues: 'why do you not leave him and stay here?' → 何不捨去而相守耶: why not leave rather than stay with him? (Beal: why not leave him); 'returned to that place' → 復至其間: also came there (no earlier visit by the merchants)
en_revised: The country is more than seven thousand *li* in circumference, and its capital city is over forty *li* in circumference. The population is dense, the crops are abundant, and the people are dark-skinned, short, and impetuous—such are their customs. The country was originally an island of gems, containing many rare treasures. Later, a girl from South India (南印度) was being sent to a neighboring country for marriage when she encountered a lion king on the road. Her escorts fled in terror, leaving the girl alone in her carriage. The lion came, saw her, and carried her away deep into the mountains, gathering fruit and hunting animals to provide for her. As time passed, she gave birth to a son and a daughter; though their forms resembled humans, their natures were violent and wicked. As the son gradually grew up, he asked his mother, "What kind of being am I? My father is a beast and my mother is a human." His mother then explained the past events to him. The son said, "Since humans and animals are different, why do you not leave him instead of staying together with him?" The mother replied, "It is not that I lack the desire, but there is no way to escape." Later, the son followed his father, climbing and traversing the mountains and valleys to observe his paths. Another day, waiting until his father had gone far away, he carried his mother and sister down to a human settlement and reached his mother's native country. They inquired after his maternal uncle's family, but the lineage was already extinct, so they took up residence in a village. When the lion king returned and did not see his wife and children, he emerged from the mountains in a violent rage, roaring through the settlements and harming many men and women passing by. The common people reported the matter to the king, who led the fourfold army and recruited fierce warriors, intending to surround and shoot the beast. When the lion saw them, he let out an angry roar, causing the men and horses to fall and collapse; no one dared to advance. After many days like this, they had achieved no success. The king again posted a reward and issued a decree: whoever could kill the lion would be granted one hundred million in gold. The son said to his mother, "Hunger and cold are difficult to endure; I wish to answer the king's recruitment, what do you think?" The mother replied, "You must not. Although he is a beast, he is still your father; if you were to kill him, could you still be called a human?" The son said, "If I do not do this, he will never leave, and he may even track us down and enter the village. Once the king finds out, we will die anyway, and he will not spare us. Why? The lion is acting violently because of you and me; how can we let one being cause trouble for so many people? Think it over carefully; it is better to answer the recruitment." Thereupon, he went. When the lion saw him, he became submissive and joyful, without any intent to harm. The son then used a sharp knife to slit his throat and rip open his belly; though subjected to such agony, the lion's deep affection and love caused him to endure it patiently without moving, and he immediately expired. The king heard this and was delighted, but wondered and asked him, "What was the reason for this?" At first, he did not speak the truth. Only after being pressed in various ways did he finally relate the whole story. The king said, "Alas! If he were not of the animal species, who could possess such a heart? Even so, I previously promised a reward and will not go back on my word. However, you have killed your father; you are a rebellious person and may no longer reside in my country." He ordered the authorities to give him much gold and treasure and to banish him to the remote wilderness. They loaded two ships, placing much gold and provisions on them, and sent them out into the sea, leaving them to drift with the currents. The ship carrying the men drifted across the sea and reached this Island of Gems; seeing that it was abundant in rare and marvelous things, they immediately settled there. Later, merchants brought their families to gather treasures and also came to that place, whereupon the men killed the merchants and kept their women. In this way, they produced children and grandchildren, and after passing through immeasurable generations, the population gradually increased, and they established a system of sovereign and subjects. Because their remote ancestor had seized and killed a lion (siṃha), the country was named accordingly. The ship carrying the women drifted across the sea to the west of Persia, where they were captured by demons and gave birth to a group of daughters; this is the present-day Great Western Women’s Country. It is also said that Siṃhala was the name of a merchant’s son who, by virtue of his great wisdom, escaped the harm of the Rākṣasa demons, later became king, came to this Island of Gems, exterminated the Rākṣasas, and established the capital, which was named after him; the account is in the *Records of the Western Regions* (Xiyu ji).  Previously, there was no Buddha-dharma in this country. One hundred years after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, the younger brother of King Aśoka (Wuyou wang), Mahinda (Mohe yintuoluo), grew weary of and abandoned sensual desires, attained the four fruits of a śramaṇa, and traveled through the air to wander and transform this country. He praised the Buddha’s teachings and manifested supernatural powers, causing the people of the country to believe and admire him, and they established saṃghārāmas. There are more than one hundred such sites, with ten thousand monks who follow the teachings of both the Mahāyāna and the Sthavira schools. The members of the clergy are solemn and respectful, their precepts and conduct are pure and bright, and they encourage one another without negligence. Beside the royal palace is the Buddha’s Tooth mūla-gandha-kuṭī (Jingshe), several hundred feet high, adorned with various treasures. A pillar is erected on top, and a great padmarāga jewel is placed at the tip of the mast; its radiance shines into the sky, and on a clear, quiet night, it can be seen from ten thousand li away. Beside it is another *mūla-gandha-kuṭī* (Jingshe), also adorned with various precious substances. Inside is a golden image, created by a former king of this country, with a precious pearl in its topknot whose value no one knows. Later, someone wished to steal this pearl, but the guards were so vigilant that he had no way to enter; he then secretly tunneled through the ground into the chamber to take it, but the image grew taller and taller, so that the thief could not reach it. The thief stepped back and said, "When the Tathāgata formerly practiced the Bodhisattva path, he did not begrudge his own body or life for the sake of all sentient beings, nor did he cling to his cities or kingdoms; why then today are you so stingy and stubborn? Thinking of this, I fear that the accounts of the past are untrue." The image then bowed its body and offered the pearl. After the man obtained it, he took it out to sell, but someone who recognized it seized him and sent him to the king. The king asked how he had obtained it. The thief replied, "The Buddha gave it to me himself," and he recounted the circumstances in detail. The king went to see for himself and found that the head of the image was still bowed. Upon witnessing this divine miracle, the king’s faith deepened further, and he used various precious gems to redeem the pearl from the thief, restoring it to the topknot of the image. It remains there to this day.

issues: 'I have therefore interviewed people' → 訪諸人口，梗概如是: impersonal/third person in the Life (he could not go in person; from inquiry the outline is thus), not a first-person speaker
en_revised: Sailing several thousand li across the sea to the south of the country, one reaches the island of Nārikela (那羅稽羅洲). The inhabitants of this island are diminutive, being just over three feet tall; they have human bodies and bird-like beaks, and they do not practice agriculture, subsisting instead on coconuts. Because the ocean waves of that country are vast and distant, he could not go there in person; inquiring of people, he obtained this general account.

issues: 'more than seventy monks from the country of Siṃhala were returning to the northwest ... they traveled' → 自達羅毘茶與師子國僧七十餘人，西北歸: the Master (understood subject) went back northwest from Drāviḍa together with seventy-odd Siṃhala monks (Beal: he went north-west in company with about seventy priests); text writes 建那補羅 without 恭 (likely a dropped character)
en_revised: From the country of Drāviḍa (達羅毘茶), together with more than seventy monks of the country of Siṃhala (師子國), he went back to the northwest to view and pay homage to the holy sites; traveling more than two thousand li, he arrived at the country of Koṅkaṇapura (恭建那補羅國). There are over one hundred monasteries and more than ten thousand monks, who study both the Great and Lesser Vehicles. The temples of the devas and the followers of non-Buddhist paths are also very numerous. Beside the city of the royal palace, there is a large monastery with over three hundred monks, all of whom are learned and erudite scholars. In its Mūlagandhakuṭī (精舍), there is the precious crown of Prince Sarvārthasiddha (一切義成太子). It is slightly less than two feet high and is kept in a precious casket; whenever a fast day arrives, it is brought out and placed on a high platform, and those who observe it with utmost sincerity often perceive miraculous light. In the monastery beside the city, there is a Mūlagandhakuṭī containing a sandalwood statue of Maitreya Bodhisattva (慈氏菩薩) that is over ten feet high; it also frequently emits auspicious light, and it is said to have been made by the Arhat Śrotaviṃśatikoṭi (二百億羅漢). To the north of the city, there is a forest of tāla trees (多羅樹) with a circumference of more than thirty li; the leaves are long and have a lustrous color, and they are highly valued by all the countries for the purpose of copying texts.

issues: 'exquisite delicacies' → 上味奇珍: the finest food and rare treasures (Beal: food of the best description, choice jewels); 奇珍 dropped
en_revised: From here, traveling north for more than a thousand *li*, one arrives at the country of Valabhī (伐臘毘國). There are more than a hundred monasteries and over six thousand monks, who study the teachings of the Saṃmitīya school of the Hīnayāna. During the time the Tathāgata was in the world, he frequently traveled to this country, and wherever he went, King Aśoka (無憂王) erected markers. The current king is of the Kṣatriya caste. He is the son-in-law of King Śīlāditya (尸羅阿迭多王) of the country of Kanyākubja (羯若鞠闍國), and his name is Dhruvabhaṭa. His nature is impetuous and his manners are careless, yet he esteems virtue, values learning, and faithfully loves the Triple Gem. Every year, he holds a great seven-day assembly, inviting monks from various countries and providing them with the finest food and rare treasures, bedding, clothing, and even medicinal supplies, ensuring that nothing is lacking.

issues: 'Samyuktābhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra (攝正法論)' and 'Lakṣaṇānusāra-śāstra (教實論)' → unfounded Sanskrit equivalents (the Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya is 雜阿毘曇心論); give the Chinese titles; 'Dharma Master' → the Master of the Law (法師)
en_revised: From here, traveling northeast for more than seven hundred *li*, one arrives at the country of Parvata (鉢伐多國). Beside the city is a large monastery with over a hundred monks, all of whom study the Mahayana; this is where the Shastra-master Jinaputra (慎那弗怛羅) formerly composed the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra-vyākhyā* (瑜伽師地釋論), and it is also the place where the Shastra-masters Bhadraruci (賢愛) and Guṇaprabha (德光) originally entered the monastic life. Furthermore, there are two or three great virtuous ones in this country whose scholarly attainments are worthy of emulation. The Master of the Law stayed there for two years to study the *Mūlābhidharma* (根本阿毘達摩), the *Shezhengfa lun* (攝正法論), and the *Jiaoshi lun* (教實論) of the Sāmmitīya school.

issues: 'Atembasila' → 阿點婆翅羅 is Audumbatira (form of the checked Xiyu ji translation; Beal: O-tin-po-chi-lo, Atyanabakela); in the Life 'from here' is Surāṣṭra (preceding sentence 從此又西還蘇剌侘國, not in this excerpt)
en_revised: From here, he traveled west again and reached the country of Audumbatira (阿點婆翅羅國). When the Tathāgata was in the world, he frequently visited this land, and King Aśoka built stūpas at every place where there were sacred traces; these all exist to this day.

issues: 'three hundred li' → 三百餘里: more than three hundred li; 'Eight hundred paces' → 八百餘步: more than eight hundred paces
en_revised: From here, traveling more than three hundred li to the northeast, one arrives at the country of Avaṇḍa (阿軬荼國). In a large forest to the northeast of the city is the old foundation of a monastery, which is where the Buddha formerly permitted the bhikṣus to wear sandals (丞縛屣). There is a stūpa built by King Aśoka. Beside it is a mūla-gandha-kuṭī (精舍), in which there is a standing Buddha image of blue stone that frequently emits light. More than eight hundred paces further to the south, in a large forest, there is a stūpa built by King Aśoka; this is where the Tathāgata once stayed and, because the night was cold, covered himself with his three robes, and where, the next morning, he permitted the bhikṣus to wear quilted garments (納衣).

issues: 'the summit of the Great Mountain (Pravaragiri)' → 大山頂: the top of a great mountain; the Sanskrit name is DM's invention; 七僧并雇人等有二十餘 may mean seven monks plus hired men, twenty-odd in all (Beal: seven priests, twenty followers); kept DM; 'they could not reach its summit' → 莫至其表: clouds and flying snow do not reach its top (Beal: the flying snow does not reach its summit)
en_revised: The king dispatched a high official with over one hundred men to escort the Master of the Law across the Snowy Mountains, carrying fodder and provisions to supply him. After traveling for seven days, they reached the top of a great mountain. The mountain consisted of overlapping ranges and perilous peaks, irregular and varied in form; some were flat and others towering, their configurations not of a single type. The ascent was arduous and difficult to describe in full. From this point on, it was impossible to ride horses, so they proceeded by leaning on staves. After another seven days, they reached a high ridge. Below the ridge was a village of about one hundred households that raised sheep; the sheep were as large as donkeys. They stayed overnight in this village and set out at midnight, having a villager ride a mountain camel to lead the way. The terrain was full of snowy ravines and icy streams; if they had not relied on the guidance of the local villager, they would have feared falling into them. By the following day, they had finally crossed the dangerous ridges. At that time, there were only seven monks and over twenty hired men, with one elephant, ten mules, and four horses. The next day they reached the foot of the ridge and followed a winding path to climb another ridge; from a distance it looked like snow, but upon reaching it, they found it was all white rocks. This ridge was the highest; although clouds gather and snow flies, they do not reach its top. It was dusk when they finally arrived at the peak, where the cold wind was so biting and severe that no one in the party could stand upright. Furthermore, the mountain had no vegetation; there were only piled rocks and clustered peaks, standing precariously like a forest of bamboo shoots. Because the mountain was so high and the wind so fierce, birds attempting to cross could not fly; only after traveling several hundred paces away from either the southern or northern side of the ridge could they finally spread their wings. Among the mountain heights in the continent of Jambudvīpa, there is none that surpasses this one.

issues: '(Himālaya)' → 兩雪山: two snowy ranges flanking the Pamir valley, not the Himālaya; gloss removed
en_revised: It is situated between the two Snowy Mountains, and also lies in the midst of the Pamir Mountains (Cōnglǐng).

en_revised: North beyond the great mountains of this country one comes to the country of Śikni (尸棄尼國).

issues: 'seven hundred li' → 七百餘里: more than seven hundred li; 'fifty li from south to north' → 五十餘里: more than fifty li; Life has 東 (east) where the Xiyu ji has 東北
en_revised: From here, traveling east through the mountains for more than seven hundred li, one arrives at the Pamir Valley (波謎羅川). The valley is over a thousand li from east to west and over a hundred li from south to north. It is situated between two snowy mountains and lies in the heart of the Onion Range (葱嶺). Wind and snow swirl there without ceasing even in spring and summer; due to the piercing cold, vegetation is sparse, crops do not grow, and the region is desolate and devoid of human traces. In the valley is a Great Dragon Lake, three hundred li from east to west and more than fifty li from south to north. It is located in the center of Jambudvīpa; the terrain is high and elevated, and the lake appears so vast that the eye cannot see its limit. Aquatic creatures of a thousand kinds and ten thousand species make a clamorous noise, as if in a marketplace of a hundred craftsmen. There are also birds standing over a zhang (丈) tall, with eggs as large as jars. These were formerly called the giant eggs of Tiaozhi (條支), and perhaps this is the place. A river branches out from the west of the lake, flowing west to the eastern border of the kingdom of Dharmasthiti (達摩悉鐵帝國), where it joins the Vakṣu River (縛芻河) and flows west into the sea; all the waters to the right also converge there. A large river branches out from the east of the lake, flowing east to the western border of the kingdom of Khāsa (佉沙國), where it joins the Sītā River (徙多河) and flows east into the sea; all the waters to the left also converge there. Beyond the mountains to the south of the valley is the kingdom of Balūra (鉢露羅國), which is rich in gold and silver, the gold being the color of fire. Furthermore, this lake is situated directly north and south of the Anavatapta Lake (阿耨池).

issues: 'country of Khasa (朅槃陀國)' → 朅槃陀 is Kharbanda (Tashkurgan), not Khasa (佉沙, Kashgar); 'serving as the source of the rivers in this country' → 為此國河源: it becomes the source of the River (the Yellow River) of this country, i.e. China (Beal: the origin of our (Yellow) river); 'Three hundred li' → 三百餘里: more than three hundred li; 從多河 is a miswriting of 徙多河 (Sītā)
en_revised: From this river valley, traveling east, ascending dangerous heights and treading upon snow, one journeys more than five hundred *li* to reach the country of Kharbanda (朅槃陀國). The city is built against a steep ridge, with the Sita River (從多河) to its north; this river flows east into the Salt Lake, runs underground, and emerges at Mount Jishi, becoming the source of the River (河) of this country, i.e. China (the Yellow River). The king is intelligent and wise, belonging to a dynasty that has endured for many years; he claims to be of the Cīna-deva-gotra (脂那提婆瞿怛羅), and in the king’s old palace, there is a monastery dedicated to the former Venerable Master Kumāralāta (童受論師). The Venerable was a native of the country of Takṣaśilā (怛叉始羅國), possessed of divine perception and extraordinary talent; he recited thirty-two thousand words daily and wrote an equal amount, mastering all doctrines and excelling in elegant composition. He authored dozens of treatises that were widely circulated, and he is the founding master of the Sautrāntika school. At that time, Aśvaghoṣa (馬鳴) in the east, Deva (提婆) in the south, Nāgārjuna (龍猛) in the west, and Kumāralāta in the north were known as the Four Suns, for they could illuminate the delusions of sentient beings. Because Kumāralāta’s reputation was so high, the former king personally led a campaign against his country to welcome him and provide him with offerings. More than three hundred *li* to the southeast of the city, one reaches a great stone cliff containing two stone chambers, in each of which an Arhat has entered the *nirodha-samāpatti* (滅盡定); they sit upright without moving, looking like emaciated men, yet they have not decayed or collapsed for over seven hundred years. The Master of the Law stayed in this country for more than twenty days.

issues: '(which in the language of Tang means the "Solar Deity of China" race)' → not in the Life passage (imported from the Xiyu ji gloss 漢日天種, and garbled); removed
en_revised: Furthermore, the king is intelligent and wise, and his kingdom has been established through a succession of rulers for many years; he claims to be of the Cīna-deva-gotra (脂那提婆瞿怛羅).

issues: 'a great mountain (Pravaragiri)' → 大山: a great mountain; Sanskrit name invented; 'thunderous earthquake' → 雷震山崩: the mountain collapsed from a thunderclap
en_revised: Two hundred li to the west of the city is a great mountain, with peaks that are very steep and lofty, upon which stands a stupa. According to an old legend, several hundred years ago, the mountain collapsed from a thunderbolt, revealing within it a bhikṣu of withered and imposing stature, sitting with eyes closed, his hair and beard thick and long, hanging down to cover his shoulders and face. A woodcutter saw him and reported it to the king. The king went in person to observe and pay homage, and as the news spread among the gentry and commoners, people from near and far gathered together, all offering worship until the accumulated flowers formed a mound. The king asked, "What kind of person is this?" A bhikṣu replied, "This is a renunciant arhat who has entered the cessation meditation (nirodha-samāpatti); as much time has passed, his hair has grown long." The king asked, "How can we rouse him and cause him to rise?" The reply was, "A body sustained by material food will collapse upon exiting meditation; it is best to first sprinkle it with ghee and milk to moisten the skin and pores, and then strike the wooden gong (ghaṇṭā) to rouse his senses, after which he may be able to rise." The king said, "Excellent!" He then followed the monk's instructions, sprinkling the milk and striking the gong. The arhat opened his eyes and looked, saying, "Who are you people, appearing in the dharma-robes?" They replied, "We are bhikṣus." He asked, "Where is my teacher, Kāśyapa Tathāgata, now?" They replied, "He has long since entered nirvāṇa." Hearing this, he was saddened. He asked again, "Has the Buddha Śākyamuni attained supreme perfect enlightenment?" They answered, "He has already attained it, benefited beings, and also passed into extinction." Having heard this, he lowered his eyebrows for a long while, then lifted his hair with his hands, rose into the air, performed great spiritual transformations, and manifested fire to cremate his own body, after which his remains fell to the ground. The king and the great assembly collected the bones and erected a stūpa; this is that very monument.

issues: 'formerly called Shule (疏勒), which is the name of its capital city' → not in the Life passage (imported from the Xiyu ji note); removed
en_revised: From here, traveling north for more than five hundred li, he reached the country of Khāsa (佉沙國).

issues: 'a great mountain (Pravaragiri)' → 大山: a great mountain; Sanskrit name invented
en_revised: To the south of the country is a great mountain; the mountain has many cave chambers. Many people from India who have attained the fruits of enlightenment have employed their supernatural powers to come here and dwell, and those who have entered into final cessation (nirvana) here are numerous. Even now, there are three arhats living in the rock caves, having entered into the meditative state of cessation; as their hair and beards gradually grow long, the monks periodically go there to shave them.

issues: 'over one hundred sangharamas' → 伽藍百所: a hundred saṃghārāmas (no 餘)
en_revised: From here, traveling eastward for more than eight hundred li, one arrives at the country of Kustana (瞿薩旦那國). The land is mostly sandy desert, yet it is suitable for grain and rich in fruit. It produces rugs and fine felt, and the workmanship of its cotton cloth is exceptionally delicate. Furthermore, the soil is rich in white jade and black jade. The climate is temperate and harmonious; the people understand ritual and righteousness, value learning, and appreciate music and rhyme. Their demeanor is refined and orderly, differing from the customs of other Hu peoples. Their writing follows that of India from afar, with only slight modifications. They revere the Buddha Dharma, possessing one hundred sangharamas and more than five thousand monks, most of whom study the Mahayana.  The king is heroic, wise, and martial, and he respects and loves those who are virtuous; he claims to be a descendant of the deity Vaisravana (毘沙門天). The king’s ancestor was the crown prince of King Ashoka (無憂王) in the country of Taksasila (怛叉始羅國). Later, having been banished to the north of the Snowy Mountains, he lived by herding livestock and following water and grass, eventually establishing his capital here. Having been without a son for a long time, he prayed at the temple of Vaisravana. A boy emerged from the forehead of the temple deity, and furthermore, a miraculous substance, sweet and fragrant like milk, grew from the ground in front of the temple. He took this to nourish the child, who subsequently grew to adulthood. When the king passed away, his successor ascended the throne; his prestige and virtue spread far and wide, and he annexed various neighboring countries. The current king is his descendant. Because the ancestor was originally nourished by the milk of the earth, the correct pronunciation in the language of Khotan (于闐) is the country of "Earth-Milk" (地乳國).

issues: '(Mahā-vālukā-maru)' → 大流沙 has no Sanskrit original here; DM's gloss removed
en_revised: From here, he again traveled east into the Great Quicksands, where the sands shift with the wind; the land lacks water and grass, and there are many perils from heat-toxins and malevolent spirits. There are no paths, and travelers going to and fro rely on the skeletal remains of humans and animals as landmarks; the terrain is rugged and difficult to traverse, just as described in the previous account. After traveling another four hundred-plus *li*, he reached the ancient kingdom of Tukhāra (覩貨邏故國).

issues: 'Two days later, the journey resumed' → 後日發引: the next day he set out (Beal: the following day he conducted him on his way); 'The Master' → the Master of the Law (法師)
en_revised: The Master of the Law stayed for seven days. When the King of Kustana (于闐) heard that the Master of the Law had arrived in his territory, he came in person to welcome and greet him. The next day he set out; the King returned to the capital ahead of time, leaving his son behind to attend to the Master. After traveling for two days, the King again dispatched high-ranking officials to welcome him, and they stayed the night forty li away from the city. The next day, the King, along with monks and laypeople, brought music, incense, and flowers to receive the Master on the left side of the road. Upon his arrival, he was invited into the city and lodged in a Hinayana Sarvāstivāda monastery.
